abide.verb type: **stative** in the living *cannot abide* sense — an attitude, not an act, so the progressive is odd: ✗ *I am abiding the noise*. Action — dynamic only in the archaic dwelling sense (*her family abode in that valley*).
abide.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the tolerate sense, where the object is obligatory (*I cannot abide people who talk*; ✗ *I cannot abide*); intransitive in the dwelling sense (*a strange quiet abides in that house*) and in the prepositional *abide by the ruling*.
abide.passive: **restricted** — the stative tolerate sense resists it: ✗ *the noise could not be abided by her*. The prepositional passive works in legal writing: *every term of the settlement was abided by*. The dwelling sense is intransitive and has none.

alight.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of motion and coming to rest (*a cardinal alit on the railing*). Keep it apart from the adjective *alight*, meaning on fire, which is not a verb form at all.
alight.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense — what is landed on or stepped out of comes after a preposition (*alight on the feeder*, *alights at the Franklin Street stop*, *alighted on a compromise*), never as a bare object: ✗ *she alit the railing*.
alight.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is no object to promote: ✗ *the railing was alit*. *The barn was alight* is the adjective, not a passive.

baby-sit.verb type: action — dynamic; a work verb, and equally at home in the informal sense of watching a process that should not need watching (*baby-sit the build*).
baby-sit.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the child or the process as object (*she baby-sat my nephews*, *he baby-sat the server all night*), intransitive when the object is left out (*I baby-sit for the Novaks most Friday nights*).
baby-sit.passive: **yes** in the transitive uses — *the twins were baby-sat by a neighbor*, *that migration got baby-sat all night*. No passive of the bare intransitive *she baby-sits on Fridays*.

backlight.verb type: action — dynamic; a causative lighting verb. The participle *backlit* has gone on to work as a plain adjective: *a backlit screen*, *a backlit keyboard*.
backlight.transitivity: **transitive** only, and the object is obligatory — *the photographer backlit her subject*; ✗ *the photographer backlit* is incomplete.
backlight.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the commoner form — *every display in the lobby is backlit around the clock*, *the keyboard had been backlit in blue*.

backslide.verb type: action — dynamic; a process verb of gradual relapse, used of dieters, believers, and institutions alike (*democratic backsliding*).
backslide.transitivity: **intransitive** in all three senses — what is lost ground on takes a preposition (*backslid on reading scores*, *backslid on every reform*), never a direct object: ✗ *she backslid her diet*.
backslide.passive: **no** — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted to subject: ✗ *the reform was backslid*. Only the noun *backsliding* carries the sense in passive-shaped writing.

beget.verb type: action — dynamic; a causative verb, formal and aphoristic (*violence begets violence*) or biblical (*Abraham begot Isaac*).
beget.transitivity: **transitive**, with an obligatory object in both senses — *cheap money can beget speculation*; ✗ *violence begets* alone says nothing.
beget.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but stilted in the causal sense (*a decade of lawsuits was begot by that decision*); the passive that Americans actually meet is the frozen archaic participle *his only begotten son*.

behold.verb type: **stative-leaning perception verb**, patterning with *see* rather than *watch*: the progressive is unnatural — ✗ *the crowd is beholding the eclipse*. Literary throughout, and imperative-only in *Behold the size of that canyon*.
behold.transitivity: **transitive**, with an obligatory object (*the crowd beheld the eclipse*, *few travelers have beheld that valley*); the frozen *lo and behold* takes no object at all.
behold.passive: **restricted** — possible only in literary register: *a sight beheld by few* passes, while a full *the eclipse was beheld by the crowd* reads as costume English.

betide.verb type: action — dynamic, but an event verb rather than a deed: something befalls a person. Archaic outside the subjunctive *woe betide*, which takes no ending (*woe betide anyone who is late*).
betide.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the person affected as object (*woe betide the student who forgets*, *great sorrow betid the household*), intransitive when the event simply occurs (*whatever may betide, we will meet again*).
betide.passive: **no** — the verb is archaic and its object is an experiencer, not a patient: ✗ *the household was betid by great sorrow* is not English in any register.

bide.verb type: action — dynamic, but alive only inside a fixed frame. *Bide one's time* is the one living use; do not confuse it with the separate regular verb *bode*, to be a sign of something (*this bodes well*).
bide.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the living idiom, where the object is fixed and possessive (*he bided his time*), intransitive in the archaic dwelling sense (*he had bode in that harbor town all winter*).
bide.passive: **no** — the idiom's object cannot be promoted: ✗ *his time was bided*. The dwelling sense is intransitive and has no passive either.

bind.verb type: action — dynamic throughout. The participle *bound* has two frozen adjectival lives that are no longer verbal: *bound to happen* (certain to) and *bound for Chicago* (headed for).
bind.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the tying, obliging, uniting, bookbinding, and dressing senses (*she bound the stack of letters*, *the contract binds both parties*), intransitive in the setting and jamming senses (*an egg helps the mixture bind*, *the drawer binds whenever the wood swells*).
bind.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the letters were bound with kitchen twine*, *both parties are bound by the contract for five years*. No passive of the intransitive *the drawer binds*, and *it was bound to happen* is an adjective, not a passive.

bleed.verb type: action — dynamic; a process verb literally (*his nose bled*) and figuratively (*the company bleeds cash*).
bleed.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the losing-blood, spreading, and blurring senses (*cheap dye bleeds in hot water*, *work bleeds into the weekend*), transitive in the draining and financial senses (*he bled the radiator*, *the fund bled investors for three years*).
bleed.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *every line on the car has been bled*, *the brakes were bled after the lines were changed*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *ten minutes were bled by his nose*.

breastfeed.verb type: action — dynamic. The participle also serves as a plain adjective in medical and parenting writing: *breastfed infants show a different gut flora*.
breastfeed.transitivity: **both** — the object is optional: transitive with the baby as object (*she breastfed both of her children*), intransitive when the activity alone is meant (*many mothers breastfeed for the first six months*).
breastfeed.passive: **yes** — *both children were breastfed for two solid years*, *the twins had been breastfed until they were weaned*.

breed.verb type: action — dynamic, causative when a breeder is behind it (*they bred quarter horses*) and simply eventive when the animals do it themselves (*rabbits breed fast*).
breed.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the selective-breeding, causing, and raising senses (*the kennel breeds only two litters a year*, *delay breeds rumor*), intransitive in the reproducing sense (*the herons have bred on that island for decades*).
breed.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *those roses had been bred for cold winters*, *he was born and bred in Tulsa*. No passive of the intransitive *rabbits breed fast*.

chide.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech-act verb, formal and journalistic where ordinary speech says *scold*.
chide.transitivity: **transitive**, with the person scolded as object (*she chides me whenever I skip breakfast*); the reason and the result follow prepositions (*chide him for a mistake*, *chided him out of buying the thing*).
chide.passive: **yes** — *he was chided for a mistake he did not make*, *the class was chided for its sloppy handwriting*. Modern American writes the passive with the regular *chided*, not ✗ *was chid*.

climb.verb type: action — dynamic; a motion verb literally (*we climb that ridge*) and a change-of-degree verb figuratively (*prices climb every summer*).
climb.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the thing scaled as object (*ivy climbs the whole north wall*), intransitive in the rising, aviation, and preposition-taking senses (*the temperature has climbed six degrees*, *he climbed into the truck*).
climb.passive: **restricted** — natural only when the object is a genuine climbing objective: *that face has been climbed only twice*. The rising senses have no passive at all: ✗ *six degrees have been climbed by the temperature*.

cling.verb type: action — dynamic but durative: it describes holding on over time rather than a single act, physically (*the toddler clung to her leg*), adhesively (*static clings to everything*), or figuratively (*he has clung to that theory for thirty years*).
cling.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense — what is held onto always follows *to* or another preposition: ✗ *she clung the railing*, only *she clung to the railing*.
cling.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is no object to promote: ✗ *the railing was clung*. Even the prepositional passive is marginal: ? *that theory has been clung to for thirty years*.

crossbreed.verb type: action — dynamic, causative when a breeder or a lab is behind it and eventive when populations mix on their own.
crossbreed.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the varieties as object (*the lab crossbred the two strains*, *growers crossbreed these apples for firmness*), intransitive when it happens without a breeder (*the two populations crossbreed wherever their ranges overlap*).
crossbreed.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *Angus and Hereford cattle have been crossbred for generations*, *the two strains were crossbred last spring*. No passive of the intransitive.

dig.verb type: action — dynamic. The 1950s slang sense of liking something (*I dig that record*) is stative in meaning, but unlike most statives it takes the progressive freely: *I'm digging this album*.
dig.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the hole or the unearthed thing as object (*they dig a new well*, *she dug out the old lease*), intransitive when the digging alone is meant or a preposition follows (*the dog dug under the fence*, *the committee has dug into the contracts*).
dig.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the well was dug in 1954*, *three more emails have been dug up*. The slang liking sense refuses it: ✗ *that record is dug by me*.

ding.verb type: action — dynamic; a sound verb in the original sense (*the elevator dings at every floor*) and an impact verb in the modern American one (*I dinged the car door*).
ding.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the denting, penalizing, and striking senses (*three schools dinged him*, *hail dinged the roof*), intransitive in the ringing sense (*timers ding all over the kitchen at six*).
ding.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *he was dinged by three schools before he got an offer*, *every corner of that table has been dinged*. No passive of the ringing sense: ✗ *the hour was dung by the clock*.

feed.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from nourishing to supplying (*two sensors feed data to the controller*). *Fed up* is a frozen adjectival participle, not a live verb form.
feed.transitivity: **all three** — intransitive of animals grazing (*deer feed at dusk*), transitive with the eater or the machine as object (*we feed the cats at six*, *he fed the parking meter*), and **ditransitive** in the supplying and sports senses (*she fed him a perfect ball*, *two sensors feed the controller data*).
feed.passive: **yes** — *the whole crowd had been fed before the speeches started*, *that stray has been fed all winter*. But *I am fed up with the noise* only looks passive: there is no active ✗ *the noise fed me up*.

fight.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of struggle, literal (*he fought in the Pacific*), interpersonal (*they fight about money*), and civic (*the union has fought three contract battles*).
fight.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when no opponent is named or one follows a preposition (*two guys fight outside that bar*, *we fought the whole drive home*), transitive with an opponent, an obstacle, or a claim as object (*crews fought the fire*, *he fought the ticket and won*).
fight.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the fire was fought for nine days*, *the rezoning had been fought for two years*. No passive of the quarreling sense: ✗ *money is fought about by them*.

find.verb type: action — dynamic in the discovery senses (*she found my keys in the freezer*); **stative** in the judging sense, which reports an opinion rather than an act — *I find the whole argument unconvincing*, and the progressive is odd there: ✗ *I am finding the argument unconvincing*.
find.transitivity: **transitive** throughout, with an obligatory object (✗ *she found* is incomplete); senses 4 and 5 add an object complement (*I find the argument unconvincing*, *the jury found him guilty on two counts*), and *find someone the time* also allows two objects.
find.passive: **yes** — *no evidence of tampering has been found*, *he was found guilty on two counts*, *the effect was found to disappear after a year*. Even the stative judging sense passivizes: *the argument was found unconvincing*.

fling.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of forceful motion, whether the force is anger, haste, or indifference (*he flung the door open and walked out*).
fling.transitivity: **transitive**, with an obligatory object (*don't fling your coat on the floor*; ✗ *don't fling*), and reflexive in the commitment sense (*she has flung herself into the new job*).
fling.passive: **yes** in the ordinary transitive sense — *a rock had been flung through the front window*, *a two-goal lead had been flung away*. The reflexive use has none: ✗ *herself was flung into the new job*.

floodlight.verb type: action — dynamic; a causative lighting verb. The participle *floodlit* also works as a plain adjective: *a floodlit field*, *a floodlit parking lot*.
floodlight.transitivity: **transitive** only, and the object is obligatory — *they floodlit the bridge for the anniversary*; ✗ *crews floodlight* is incomplete.
floodlight.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the usual form — *the stadium had been floodlit long before kickoff*, *the plaza has been floodlit every December since 1998*.

force-feed.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: it makes someone take in food, or figuratively information they did not ask for (*he force-feeds his students dates and names*).
force-feed.transitivity: **transitive**, and **ditransitive** in the figurative sense with both a recipient and a thing (*advertisers have force-fed us the same jingle*); the literal sense takes one object (*the vet force-fed the puppy*).
force-feed.passive: **yes** — *the calf had been force-fed until it could nurse on its own*, *we have been force-fed the same jingle all month*.

get.verb type: action — dynamic in the obtaining, fetching, and arriving senses; **linking (copular)** with an adjective, where it means *become* (*it got dark*, *the weather has gotten worse*); **auxiliary-like** in the informal passive *get hired, get married, get hurt*; and **stative** in *have got* (possession) and *have got to* (obligation), which are present-tense idioms, not perfects.
get.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the obtaining, understanding, and catching senses (*she got a raise*, *nobody got the joke*), **ditransitive** in *get me a chair*, and intransitive or linking with an adjective, particle, or preposition (*it got dark*, *we had gotten halfway to Reno*, *they get by on one income*).
get.passive: **restricted** — *get* itself barely passivizes: ✗ *a raise was gotten by her*, and the possessive idiom refuses outright, ✗ *a spare key is had got by me*. What *get* actually does is build other verbs' passives: *they got married in a courthouse*, *two people got hurt in the pileup*.

grind.verb type: action — dynamic; a process verb of crushing and abrasion, and the source of the noun in *the daily grind*. Keep it apart from the separate regular verb *ground, grounded* (*the flight was grounded*, never ✗ *the flight was ground*).
grind.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the crushing, sharpening, and wearing-down senses (*I grind the beans right before brewing*, *the commute grinds people down*), intransitive in the grating and halting senses (*the gears ground every time he shifted*, *traffic had ground to a stop*).
grind.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the blade had been ground down to almost nothing*, *coffee has been ground into the carpet*. No passive of *traffic ground to a halt*, and none of the homophonous *grounded*.

hang.verb type: action — dynamic when you put something up (*he hung his jacket*); the intransitive twin is closer to a state of position (*the portrait had hung in that hallway since 1962*). The computing sense is eventive: *the app hangs whenever I open that file*.
hang.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the suspending, executing, and ending-a-call senses (*we hang the wreath*, *the state hanged him in 1892*), intransitive when something dangles, looms, freezes, or in the phrasals *hang out* and *hang on* (*smoke has hung over the valley for a week*).
hang.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *new blinds have been hung in every room*. The execution sense keeps the regular form in the passive too: *three men had been hanged before the pardon arrived*, never ✗ *three men had been hung*. No passive of the intransitive *a single bulb hangs over the table*.

heave.verb type: action — dynamic; effortful motion, whether you supply the effort (*he heaved the box onto the truck*) or something else does (*the sidewalk has heaved where the roots got under it*).
heave.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the lifting sense and in the fixed *heave a sigh* (*he heaved a sigh and signed it anyway*), intransitive in the rising-and-falling, retching, and nautical senses (*her shoulders heaved*, *the freighter hove into view*).
heave.passive: **restricted** — the lifting sense passivizes (*every sandbag on that pile has been heaved onto the dock*), but the fixed collocation resists (✗ *a sigh was heaved by her*) and the nautical and retching senses are intransitive with no passive at all.

hold.verb type: action — dynamic in the grasping, staging, and detaining senses (*they held the election in November*); **stative** in the capacity, possession, and belief senses, which resist the progressive: ✗ *the tank is holding forty gallons*, ✗ *he is holding two patents*, ✗ *most economists are holding the opposite view*.
hold.transitivity: **both** — transitive in most senses (*he held the ladder*, *police held him overnight*, *hold your breath*), intransitive in the load-bearing and validity senses (*that rope holds about three hundred pounds*, *the rule holds in every case we tested*).
hold.passive: **restricted** — the dynamic senses go freely (*the election was held in November*, *the shipment has been held at customs*), and so does the occupying sense in formal registers (*a majority stake is held by the family*). But the containing sense refuses outright: ✗ *forty gallons are held by the tank*, ✗ *two hundred people have been held by that room*.

interbreed.verb type: action — dynamic, eventive when populations mix on their own and causative when a breeder or a station drives it.
interbreed.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the ordinary biological sense (*the two populations interbreed wherever their ranges overlap*, *the valley families had interbred for generations*), transitive when someone causes it (*breeders interbreed the lines to fix the coat color*).
interbreed.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *wheat varieties have been interbred since the 1930s*, *the lines are interbred to fix the coat color*. No passive of the intransitive *wolves and coyotes interbred*.

lead.verb type: action — dynamic; guiding literally (*the ranger led us up the switchbacks*), directing an organization (*she leads the team*), and causing in *lead to* (*one question led to another*).
lead.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a person, a group, or a life as object (*he led the department for six years*, *they lead a quiet life*), intransitive in the road, scoring, and *lead to* senses (*this trail should lead you straight to the falls*, *they lead the division by four games*).
lead.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the department was led by her for six years*, *he was led on for months*, *we were led to the wrong house entirely*. No passive of *lead to*: ✗ *a lot of confusion has been led to*.

light.verb type: action — dynamic. The participle *lighted* doubles as an adjective in front of a noun (*a lighted match*, *a lighted window*), where *lit* is less at home.
light.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the igniting and illuminating senses (*he lit the grill with a long match*, *that one lamp lights the whole room*), intransitive in *light up*, *light on*, and the dated slang *light out* (*her whole face lights up when he calls*, *a moth had lit on the screen door*).
light.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *every candle on the table has been lit*, *the runway had been lit before the plane turned in*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *California was lit out for*.

meet.verb type: action — dynamic in the encountering, convening, and receiving senses; closer to **stative** in the requirement sense, which states a fact rather than an event: ✗ *this proposal is meeting all three conditions*.
meet.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a person, a standard, or an arrival as object (*I met her standing in line at the DMV*, *this proposal meets all three conditions*, *she met us at baggage claim*), intransitive when the parties are the joint subject (*we meet every other Thursday*, *the two trails meet just above the falls*).
meet.passive: **restricted** — the requirement sense passivizes best of all: *all three conditions are met*, *the deadline was met by about four minutes*, and so does the receiving sense: *we were met at baggage claim*. The plain encountering sense resists: ✗ *she was met by me standing in line at the DMV*.

mislead.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: it produces a false impression, deliberately or not. The participle *misleading* has become an ordinary adjective, commoner than the verb itself.
mislead.transitivity: **transitive**, with the deceived person as object (*the label misled thousands of buyers*); the object may be dropped when the general effect is the point (*these charts mislead more than they explain*).
mislead.passive: **yes** — *thousands of buyers were misled by the label*, *we had been misled about the distance to the beach*, *nobody has been misled about the price*.

misunderstand.verb type: **stative** — like *understand*, it names a state of comprehension rather than an activity, so the progressive is limited to the ongoing-error reading (*I think I'm misunderstanding you*); ✗ *she is misunderstanding my email twice* is not available.
misunderstand.transitivity: **transitive**, with the words, the material, or the person misread as object (*half the class misunderstood the assignment*, *critics have misunderstood her work from the start*); the object is dropped only when context supplies it (*sorry, I misunderstood*).
misunderstand.passive: **yes**, and the passive is very common — *her work has been misunderstood from the start*, *the terms had been misunderstood before anyone signed*. The participle is also a plain adjective: *a misunderstood kid*.

outfight.verb type: action — dynamic; a comparative verb built on *fight*, meaning to fight better than the other side, mostly in sportswriting.
outfight.transitivity: **transitive**, with the opponent as an obligatory object — *he outfought a taller opponent for twelve rounds*; ✗ *smaller crews sometimes outfight* is incomplete.
outfight.passive: **yes**, though the active is far commoner — *the favorites had been outfought for most of the tournament*, *he was outfought on the inside for eight rounds*.

outshine.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the figurative *outshine the lead* and the literal *outshine every star*; no linking or stative use
outshine.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory, since you always outshine someone or something: ✗ *the understudy outshone* is incomplete
outshine.passive: **yes** — *the lead was outshone by the understudy*, *everything else on the menu has been outshone by that one dessert*

overfeed.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, of feeding animals and of oversupplying a system (*cheap credit overfed the housing market*)
overfeed.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory: ✗ *new owners overfeed* is incomplete without *their fish*
overfeed.passive: **yes** — *the fish are overfed by almost every new owner*, *the carburetor was overfed by a stuck float*. The participle also works attributively: *an overfed cat*.

overhang.verb type: **stative** in the positional sense — *those branches overhang the driveway* reports where something is, not something done; the figurative *debt overhangs the company* is stative too
overhang.transitivity: **transitive** — what is overhung is named: *overhang the driveway*, *overhang every conversation*
overhang.passive: **restricted** — the descriptive passive is fine (*a trail overhung by a dead limb*, *the porch was overhung with vines*), but because the verb is stative there is no event to passivize: ✗ *the driveway was overhung by the branches yesterday* reads oddly

overshoot.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: passing a point (*we overshot the exit*), exceeding a figure (*costs overshot the estimate*), and landing long
overshoot.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the ordinary uses (*overshoot the runway*, *overshoot their budgets*), intransitive in aviation (*if you overshoot, go around*)
overshoot.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the runway was overshot in the rain*, *the target had been overshot for six straight quarters*. No passive of the intransitive *if you overshoot*.

plead.verb type: action — a speech-act verb, dynamic in every sense: entering a plea, begging, arguing a case, offering an excuse
plead.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with a preposition when it means beg (*plead with him*, *plead for more time*), transitive with a fixed complement elsewhere (*plead guilty*, *plead the Fifth*, *plead the matter in federal court*); note ✗ *plead to be guilty*
plead.passive: **restricted** — natural where a case or a defense is the object (*the issue has been pled three times*, *insanity was pleaded*), but the fixed complements resist: ✗ *not guilty was pled by him*, and the *plead with* sense is intransitive and has no passive at all

reshoot.verb type: action — dynamic, a straightforward repetition verb built on *shoot*
reshoot.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is normally obligatory (*reshoot the ending*), though it can go unexpressed when the scene is understood: *we reshoot anything the client flags*
reshoot.passive: **yes** — *the ending was reshot twice*, *half the movie has been reshot*

rewind.verb type: action — dynamic: winding tape back, replaying a moment in your head, or rewinding a motor coil
rewind.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a tape, a conversation, or an armature (*he rewound the tape*), intransitive in the figurative *let's rewind to the part where you agreed to pay* and the interjection *rewind, say that again*
rewind.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the armature was rewound by hand*, *the generator had been rewound twice*

shine.verb type: action — dynamic, though the light senses are close to a continuous state (*the porch light shines all night*); no linking use
shine.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when it means give off light, gleam, or excel (*the sun shone*, *she shone in the second act*), transitive when it means aim a light or polish (*he shined his phone into the crawlspace*, *she shined the silver*)
shine.passive: **restricted** — yes in the transitive senses, and there the past is the regular *shined*: *his shoes are shined every Sunday*, *a spotlight has been shined on every car*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *all week was shone by the sun*.

shoot.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from firing a weapon to filming to a plant putting out shoots
shoot.transitivity: **both**, and **ditransitive** in one informal sense — intransitive in *pain shot up my arm* and *the vines shot six feet*, transitive in *someone shot out the streetlight* and *they shoot the commercial in Utah*, ditransitive in *shoot me an email*
shoot.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *he was shot in the arm*, *the whole scene had been shot before the rain came*, *the proposal was shot down in ten minutes*. The ditransitive resists: ✗ *I was shot an email* is not idiomatic; and the intransitive *kids shoot out of that school* has no passive.

sit.verb type: action in *sit down*, but **stative** in the situated and idle senses — *the house sits on two acres*, *that box sat in the garage for six years* report position, not activity
sit.transitivity: **intransitive** — *sit* never takes a direct object the way *set* does: *I sit down* but *I set the vase down*; ✗ *set down and relax* is dialect. Objects appear only with particles and prepositions: *sit through a slideshow*, *sit out the season*, *sit on the board*.
sit.passive: **no** — the verb is intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *that chair has been sat in by her for twenty years* is not idiomatic English. Even the phrasal uses resist: ✗ *four hours of testimony were sat through*.

slide.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, including the gradual *ratings slide every year*
slide.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when something moves or declines by itself (*the truck slid into the ditch*, *the stock slid eleven percent*), transitive when you push something (*he slid the envelope under the door*)
slide.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the envelope was slid under the door*, *the same note has been slid across my desk twice*. No passive of the intransitive *the stock slid*.

sling.verb type: action — dynamic: throwing casually, hanging loosely, and the fixed *sling hash*, *sling mud*
sling.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory in every sense: *sling the strap over your shoulder*, *sling mud*; ✗ *he slung* alone is incomplete
sling.passive: **yes** — *a rope had been slung across the creek*, *mud has been slung at her for a decade*

slink.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of manner of motion: moving furtively, slinking off, moving sinuously
slink.transitivity: **intransitive** — it takes a direction or a particle but never an object: *slink along the fence line*, *slink off*; ✗ *he slunk the hallway*
slink.passive: **no** — an intransitive verb has no object to promote, so there is no passive at all: ✗ *the parking lot was slunk off toward*

sneak.verb type: action — dynamic: going somewhere unnoticed, taking something secretly, sneaking up on someone
sneak.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with a direction (*he snuck out the back door*), transitive with a thing taken or done on the sly (*she snuck a cookie off the tray*, *sneak a peek*)
sneak.passive: **restricted** — possible but informal where there is an object: *three extra chairs had been snuck into the room*. The *sneak up on* frame is awkward in the passive (✗ *I was snuck up on by the deadline*), and the plain intransitive *kids sneak into the theater* has none.

speed.verb type: action — dynamic: moving fast, driving over the limit, or making something happen sooner. The traffic-offense sense lives mostly in the progressive: *she was speeding*.
speed.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the movement and offense senses (*the cab sped through the intersection*), transitive in the causative one (*antibiotics have sped his recovery*, *they speeded up production*)
speed.passive: **restricted** — the causative sense passivizes stiffly but legitimately: *approval of a dozen projects was sped by the new law*, *production was speeded up*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *that street is sped down every night*.

spin.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: rotating, twisting fiber, spinning a web, spinning the numbers
spin.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when something turns or a head swims (*the wheels spin*, *my head spins*), transitive when you turn it or make it (*spin the wheel*, *spin wool*, *spin the numbers*)
spin.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *thread has been spun on this river since 1840*, *a bad quarter was spun into a story about long-term investment*. No passive of *my head spins*.

spit.verb type: action — dynamic: ejecting saliva, spitting something out, an engine spitting smoke, or a line of speech spat in anger
spit.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the core sense (*don't spit on the floor*) and in *the fire spat*, transitive with what leaves the mouth (*he spat out the seed*, *she spat the words at him*)
spit.passive: **restricted** — grammatical where there is an object but rarely used: *the pill had been spat into a napkin*, *grease has been spat on that wall for years*. No passive of the intransitive *he spat on the sidewalk*.

spotlight.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the literal lighting and the figurative singling out
spotlight.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory: *spotlight local musicians*, *spotlight the podium*; ✗ *the report spotlighted* is incomplete
spotlight.passive: **yes** — *three failing districts were spotlighted in the report*, *the podium was spotlit*, *deer have been spotlit on that road to catch poachers*

stand.verb type: action in *stand up*, **stative** in the situated and in-force senses (*the barn stands where the original house was*, *my offer stands*), and **linking** in *stand accused*, *stand trial-ready*, *stand corrected*
stand.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the core senses (*we stand for the anthem*, *the record stood for forty years*), transitive when you set something upright (*he stood the bike against the fence*) or tolerate something (*I can't stand the smell*)
stand.passive: **restricted** — fine for the physical sense: *all the chairs have been stood on the tables*. The tolerate sense resists like other stative verbs: ✗ *the smell can't be stood*; and *stand trial*, *stand to lose*, and the situated sense have no passive at all.

stave.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses: holding something off (*stave off bankruptcy*) and smashing a hole in a hull
stave.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory in both: *stave off the worst of it*, *stave a wooden hull*
stave.passive: **yes** — and the nautical sense lives mostly in the passive: *the hull was stove in*, *the bow was stove in by the ice*. The phrasal sense passivizes too, always regular: *three takeover attempts have been staved off*.

stick.verb type: action — dynamic when you attach, push, or place something; closer to **stative** in *the drawer sticks in humid weather* and *the name stuck*, which describe a condition rather than an act
stick.transitivity: **both** — transitive when you attach or place (*he stuck a note on the fridge*, *stick it in the drawer*), intransitive when something adheres, jams, or takes hold (*these labels stick to anything*, *none of the accusations have stuck*)
stick.passive: **restricted** — yes in the transitive senses, and *be stuck with* is idiomatic and almost always passive: *I have been stuck with his old laptop for two years*, *we were stuck with the cleanup*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *for life is stuck by nicknames like that*.

sting.verb type: action — dynamic: a wasp stinging, salt water stinging a cut, criticism stinging, a dealership stinging you for money
sting.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the person or part affected (*a wasp stung him on the wrist*), intransitive when the sensation is reported alone (*remarks like that sting for years*, *salt water stings*)
sting.passive: **yes**, and the last two senses live largely in the passive — *he was stung by the review*, *we got stung for an extra night*, *he has been stung by that dealership before*

strike.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: hitting, walking out, a clock sounding the hour, striking a deal. The *strike someone as* frame is the one near-stative use: *that name strikes me as familiar*.
strike.transitivity: **both** — transitive in most senses (*the car struck a guardrail*, *they struck a bargain*, *the judge struck the paragraph*), intransitive in the labor sense and in *disaster struck*, *lightning can strike twice*
strike.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *a deal was struck over lunch*, *the remark was stricken from the record* (the older participle survives here), *two of the four claims have been struck*. No passive of the intransitive *the teachers struck*, and ✗ *I am struck as by that name* for the impression frame.

string.verb type: action — dynamic: hanging a line, threading beads, fitting strings, stringing someone along. *Strung out* has frozen into an adjective — *he looked strung out*.
string.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory in every sense: *string lights*, *string the beads*, *string that racket*, *string us along*
string.passive: **yes** — *a banner was strung across Main Street*, *cable has been strung to the back of the property*, *we were strung along with vague promises*

swing.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses: hanging and moving, wielding in an arc, turning sharply, opinion shifting, and the informal *swing the down payment*
swing.transitivity: **both** — intransitive when something moves by itself (*the gate swings shut*, *the vote swung against the proposal*), transitive when you move it or bring it off (*she has swung that ax all morning*, *she swung two weeks off in August*)
swing.passive: **restricted** — natural enough with an object (*the truck was swung around and backed in*, *better deals have been swung with less*), but no passive of the intransitive senses or of *swing by*: ✗ *the office was swung by before the storm*

tread.verb type: action — dynamic: walking, trampling, treading water, treading carefully
tread.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a route or a surface (*hikers tread that same route*, *someone trod mud across the kitchen*, *tread water*), intransitive with a preposition or an adverb (*tread on the seedlings*, *tread carefully*)
tread.passive: **yes**, and the passive prefers the other participle — *trodden*: *the grass had been trodden down to bare dirt*, *a well-trodden path*. ✗ *Carefully was trod* — the adverbial uses have no passive.

troubleshoot.verb type: action — dynamic: tracing and fixing a fault in a machine, a network, or an organization
troubleshoot.transitivity: **both** — transitive with what is being fixed (*she troubleshot the printer*, *they troubleshot the whole rollout*), intransitive when the work itself is meant (*he troubleshoots for a living*)
troubleshoot.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but avoided, because the participle *troubleshot* already makes American writers uneasy: *this same error has been troubleshot twice today* is dictionary-correct, and most writers rewrite it around *troubleshooting*

unbind.verb type: action — dynamic: untying, freeing from an obligation, taking a binding apart. *Unbound* is also a common adjective — *unbound pages*, *unbound by precedent*.
unbind.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory: *unbind the stack*, *unbind them from that contract*; ✗ *he unbound* is incomplete
unbind.passive: **yes** — *the whole bundle has been unbound*, *the whole run has been unbound for rebinding*, *he has been unbound from the noncompete*

understand.verb type: **stative** — a mental-state verb, not an activity, and it normally rejects the progressive: ✗ *I am understanding the terms*, though *I'm not understanding you* turns up in speech
understand.transitivity: **transitive** — with a noun phrase (*understand the terms*, *understand three languages*) or a clause (*I understand you're leaving in June*); the object can be left out when it is recoverable: *I understand*
understand.passive: **restricted** — like other stative verbs it resists the ordinary personal passive: ✗ *the terms are understood by me* is not how you report your own grasp. The impersonal and grammatical uses are standard, though: *it has always been understood that seniority decides*, *the subject is understood*.

unwind.verb type: action — dynamic: uncoiling, relaxing, or dismantling a financial position in stages
unwind.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a cord or a trade (*he unwound the extension cord*, *the bank unwound the hedge*), intransitive when something uncoils itself or a person relaxes (*the hose has unwound across the yard*, *I unwind with a book*)
unwind.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the hedge was unwound over three weeks*, *two of these deals have been unwound by regulators*. No passive of *she unwound on the porch*.

uphold.verb type: action — dynamic: confirming a ruling, maintaining a standard, or physically holding something up
uphold.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory: *uphold the verdict*, *uphold the law*; ✗ *the court upheld* is incomplete
uphold.passive: **yes**, and the legal sense is commonest in the passive — *the verdict was upheld*, *every one of his rulings has been upheld by the board*

win.verb type: action — dynamic: coming first, gaining something by effort, winning someone over, winning out
win.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a contest or a prize (*she won the district title*), intransitive without one (*they win about half their home games*). Watch the split with *beat*: you win a game but you beat a team — ✗ *we won them*.
win.passive: **yes** — *the contract was won on price alone*, *the seat was won back in the next election*, *every skeptic in that department has been won over*. No passive of the intransitive *they win about half*.

wind.verb type: action in the coiling and clock senses, but **stative** in *the road winds through six miles of switchbacks*, which describes a shape rather than a motion
wind.transitivity: **both** — transitive when you coil or tighten something (*she wound the yarn into a ball*, *he wound the watch*), intransitive when a road or a river takes a twisting course and in *wind up at a diner*, *the party wound down*
wind.passive: **restricted** — yes in the transitive senses: *that clock has not been wound since Grandpa died*, *tape has been wound around that handle three times*, *the company's affairs have been wound up*. No passive of the stative *the river has wound through this valley*.

withhold.verb type: action — dynamic: keeping back information or consent, deducting tax, holding back a reaction
withhold.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory: *withhold evidence*, *withhold taxes*, *withhold judgment*; ✗ *the agency withheld* is incomplete unless the object is recoverable from context
withhold.passive: **yes** — *four pages of the report were withheld*, *taxes are withheld from every paycheck*, *comment was withheld for three days*

withstand.verb type: **stative** in its commonest use — *these panels withstand winds over a hundred miles an hour* states a property of the panels, not something they do, and the progressive is odd: ✗ *the panels are withstanding a property test*. It reads as an action only of a one-time event: *the seawall withstood three hurricanes*.
withstand.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory: *withstand the pressure*, *withstand scrutiny*; ✗ *the bridge has withstood* is incomplete
withstand.passive: **restricted** — grammatical but stiff and rarely written, because the verb describes the subject's capacity rather than an action done to the object: ✗ *three hurricanes were withstood by the seawall* and ✗ *that kind of scrutiny is withstood by few arguments* both read badly. Keep it active.

wring.verb type: action — dynamic: twisting out liquid, extracting something under pressure, wringing your hands, wringing a neck
wring.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is obligatory in every sense: *wring the shirt out*, *wring a raise out of management*, *wring your hands*
wring.passive: **yes** — *every towel in the house has been wrung out*, *a raise was wrung out of management*, *every dollar had been wrung out of the budget*. The fixed *wring one's hands* stays active.
